You’re not dumb—that stuff is just a lot to hold in your head at once. I’ll break Big-O down with simple ideas and concrete examples.

Big picture: Big-O is a way to describe how the running time (or space) of an algorithm grows as the input gets bigger. We only care about the big stuff that matters when n is large, and we ignore constants and tiny details.

1) Quick intuition about common cases
- O(1) — constant: the time doesn’t depend on n at all. Example: getting the first item in an array (assuming you know the index).
- O(log n) — logarithmic: you keep cutting the problem roughly in half each step. Example: binary search in a sorted array.
- O(n) — linear: you do something once for each item. Example: counting how many items are in a list.
- O(n log n) — n times log n: you do a linear amount of work, but this work itself involves a log n factor. A classic example: efficient sorting like mergesort or heapsort.
- O(n^2) — quadratic: nested loops over n items. Example: comparing every pair of items.
- O(2^n), O(n!) — exponential and factorial growth: problems that blow up very quickly; usually not scalable for large n.

2) O(n log n) in a simple, concrete way
Think of a sorting algorithm like mergesort:
- The algorithm splits the list in half over and over, which gives you about log2(n) “levels” of splitting.
- At each level, you do O(n) work to merge the halves back together.
- Total work = O(n) per level × O(log n) levels = O(n log n).

Other way to think: you do n items, and for each item you do a task that costs roughly log n steps because of the way you structure the work. The product is n log n.

3) Amortized analysis in plain terms
Idea: look at a sequence of operations, not just one. Some operations might be cheap, a few might be expensive, but the average cost per operation over the whole sequence is what we call the amortized cost.

Example: dynamic array growth (the classic amortized case)
- Suppose an array starts with capacity 1. If you add an element when it’s full, you allocate a bigger array (say double the size) and copy old elements over (that copy cost is the expensive part).
- If you track costs over a series of appends, you’ll see most appends cost 1 (just putting the new item). Occasionally you pay a bigger cost to resize and copy.
- Over a long sequence, the total cost grows only about 2k for k appends. So the average cost per append is about 2, i.e., O(1) amortized.

A tiny concrete sequence (start with capacity 1):
- Append 1st item: cost 1 (no resize)
- Append 2nd item: resize to 2 (copy 1) + insert (cost 2)
- Append 3rd item: cost 1
- Append 4th item: resize to 4 (copy 2) + insert (cost 3)
- Append 5th–8th: cost 1 each
Total cost after 8 appends = 15. Average ≈ 15/8 ≈ 1.9 per append. So we say the operation is O(1) amortized.

Key takeaway: amortized analysis looks at the total cost of many operations and divides by how many operations there were. Even if some operations are expensive, the average can still be constant.

4) Quick practice ideas
- What’s the Big-O of:
  a) A single for loop that runs n times doing O(1) work? -> O(n)
  b) A for loop over i from 1 to n, and inside it a for loop over j from 1 to n? -> O(n^2)
  c) A loop that runs from 1 to n, inside it a binary search on a sorted array (log n) steps? -> O(n log n)
- What’s the amortized cost of appending n items to a dynamic array that doubles in size when full? Think in totals: total cost is about 2n, so amortized O(1) per append.

Great question. There are two ways to build a heap from an unsorted array, and they have different time costs.

1) The two methods
- Top-down (inserts): Start with an empty heap and insert each of the n elements one by one. Each insert costs O(log k) where k is the current size, so total time is O(n log n).
- Bottom-up (Floyd’s build-heap): Treat the array as a heap already and “fix down” every non-leaf node from right to left, starting at floor(n/2) - 1 down to 0. Each fix-down (heapify) moves an element down at most a certain number of levels. This method takes O(n) total.

Your book is talking about the bottom-up method, which is why you get O(n) instead of O(n log n).

2) Why bottom-up is linear (intuition plus a bit of math)
- Think of the heap as a tree in the array. Nodes near the bottom are almost already correct; they might move just a few steps. Nodes near the top could move more steps, but there are very few of them.
- More concretely: when you heapify a node at height h (how far it could move down), it costs about O(h) work. How many nodes have height h? About n / 2^{h+1} of them.
- Total work is roughly the sum over all heights h of (number of nodes at height h) × (cost per node) = sum_{h ≥ 0} (n / 2^{h+1}) × h.
- This sum is a constant multiple of n. In fact, it’s bounded by something like 2n, so the total time is O(n). That’s why the bottom-up build is linear.

3) Quick numeric intuition
- There are many leaves (bottom level) that cost almost nothing to heapify.
- There are fewer nodes a couple of levels up, and they cost a bit more.
- There are very few nodes at the very top, and they can cost more, but they’re few enough that the extra cost doesn’t push the total above a constant factor of n.

4) When it’s not O(n)
- If you really do insert each element into an initially empty heap (the top-down method), you get O(n log n) total.
- So the key difference is the order and the amount of work actually done at each node during the build.

  - So Case 1 applies: T(n) = Θ(n^{log_2 3}) ≈ Θ(n^{1.585}).

Part 2) The KMP preprocessing (the failure/prefix function)
What it’s computing
- The prefix function (often called pi or lps) for a pattern P of length m tells you, for each position i in P, the length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix of P[0..i].
- In plain terms: for the portion of the pattern you’ve matched so far, pi tells you the largest amount of that match you can reuse if you get a mismatch next.

How it helps you skip characters
- When you’re scanning the text, you keep q = how many characters of P you’ve matched so far.
- On a mismatch after having matched q characters, you don’t go back to the start of P. you reset q to pi[q-1], which tells you how many characters at the end of your current match still align with the beginning of P.
- Then you continue comparing T[i] with P[q], so you effectively “shift” the pattern by just the right amount and avoid re-checking a lot of characters.

A small worked example (pattern up to a point)
- Pattern P = "ABCDABD" (length m = 7)
- Compute pi:
  - pi = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0]
  - Intuition: for prefixes, the longest border grows to 1, then 2, then drops to 0 at the end.
- How a mismatch uses pi in the search
  - Suppose you’ve matched "ABCDA" (q = 5) and see a mismatch on the next text character where P[5] = 'B' but you got something else.
  - You set q = pi[5-1] = pi[4] = 1. Now you’ve only matched the first character 'A' of the pattern so far, and you continue comparing the next text character with P[1].
  - This lets you reuse that one character 'A' instead of starting over from the beginning of P.

Concrete quick walk-through with a short text (optional)
- Text T = "ABCABCDABD" and P = "ABCDABD" with pi as above.
  - Start with q = 0.
  - Scan chars, updating q when they match.
  - On a mismatch, use q = pi[q-1] to drop back to the longest border you can reuse.
  - When q reaches m, you found a match; set q = pi[m-1] to look for the next one.

Why this is powerful
- It guarantees each text character is processed at most a constant number of times (once on a forward pass, plus possibly a couple of small fallbacks). This gives the overall O(n + m) time for searching.
